METAPHOR, PSYCHOANALYTIC PROCESS, TRANSFERENCE, DEVELOPMENTAL RELATION

In this paper, the author highlights some aspects of the psychoanalytic process through the perspective of poetic metaphors. In reading new metaphors, we often become bewildered. A literal reading, and a first hand meaning, comes to nothing. A concrete reference, as well as truth, is likewise destroyed. On the ruins of these literary dimensions, however, a second hand reading, meaning, world, and truth may be formed. To take a step from literal understanding to a metaphoric one is demanding, as the former provides safety. The same is true of the position of the psychoanalytic patient. He or she needs to leave an idiosyncratic, well known, way of apprehending world and others, to take perspectives never tried before. The challenges and vulnerabilities the patient meets when facing the possibilities of starting a psychoanalytic process are compared to the position of the reader of poetic metaphors. The argument is illustrated with a psychoanalytical case.

Yanxiu Zhang

Yanxiu Zhang

yanxiu.zhang.18@ucl.ac.uk

Yanxiu Zhang   Doctoral research student (PhD in Psychoanalytic Studies) in the Psychoanalysis Unit at University College London. He was previously a postgraduate student at the same institution, where he attained a Master's in Theoretical Psychoanalytic Studies. His PhD thesis aims to offer a conceptualization of ‘the familiar’ within psychoanalysis. He is also interested in psychoanalytic explanations of social behaviours and attitudes.
COVID-19, FAMILIAR, LOCKDOWN, PSYCHOANALYSIS, UNCANNY

In the shadow of the COVID-19 pandemic, familiar life may be said to have become unequivocally altered as a result of the diffuse death threat posed by the virus and the unprecedented experience of a global lockdown. The unexpected superposition of familiarity and unfamiliarity can be linked to the psychoanalytic notion of the uncanny. For Freud, the uncanny was considered a derivative of the reappearance of the repressed, whose context is dominated by the alien nature of the repression. I suggest that a further perspective can be implied—that the sudden disruption of what is familiar is traumatic and engenders a sense of the uncanny. Reflecting on the COVID-19 pandemic, this dynamic can be identified in the following aspects: (i) an overwhelming intrusion of an unfamiliar virus upon familiar life, encouraging paranoid denial and projection of the threat and increasing the tendency to stigmatise; (ii) a continuous re-manifestation of hidden familiarities, both repressed individual conflicts and collective inequalities, illustrating the fragility of the ‘norm’; and (iii) the sudden disruption of an adopted belief (that the virus is beatable), and reconfrontation with the threat of death following lockdown failure.

New Light on the Squiggle Game: The Unexpected in Sufficient Safety in the Treatment of an Adolescent

Johanna Velt and Anne Tirilly

Anne Tirilly

veltjohanna1@gmail.com

Anne Tirilly   Speech therapist, a psychologist and a member of the Société Psychanalytique de Paris. She works at the Centre for Consultation and PsychoanalyticTherapy (CCTP) Jean Favreau in Paris and has her private practice in Athis-Mons (Essonne). She is interested in the similarities and differences in the epistemologies underpinning speech therapy and psychoanalytic treatment, therapeutic adjustments in the treatment of children and adolescents, and the concepts of latency, illusion and disillusionment in psychoanalytic treatment. She has published ‘Deux métiers. Orthophoniste ou psychanalyste, il faut choisir!’
PSYCHOANALYSIS, PSYCHOTHERAPY, SQUIGGLE GAME

In this article, we discuss the technique of the Squiggle Game (SG) and aim to shed new light on it by illustrating it with a clinical vignette. We present the case of a depressed adolescent for whom the use of SG as a wildcard avoids traumatic repetition and allows the creation of a therapeutic space that contains the paradox of guaranteed safety and the use of the unexpected. We begin by recalling the SG technique invented by Winnicott and then our own use of this technique. We then describe the clinical situation of a young depressed adolescent. We then discuss the therapeutic effects observed, linking them to the recognition of the need for security. We describe how the SG joker reduces patient– therapist asymmetry, helps to moderate interpretation and encourages a side-by-side situation. In the case of adolescents, their narcissistic fragility makes psychotherapeutic approaches difficult, so long-term SG offers a technical way of taking account of the need for security that this fragility entails. We depart from Winnicott by offering the SG technique over a long period of therapy, and we make theoretical and clinical suggestions based on our original use of SG.

PSYCHIATRIC MEDICATION, ANTIDEPRESSANTS, SELECTIVE SEROTONIN RE-UPTAKE INHIBITORS, PSYCHOTHERAPY, PSYCHOTHERAPY PROCESS, MEDICATION ADVERSE EFFECTS

Many patients enter psychotherapy while being on antidepressant medication. This article outlines and discusses the main effects of antidepressant medication both on the patient and on the psychotherapy process. Although widely prescribed, the effectiveness of antidepressant medication is still open to debate, and several authors have questioned whether it is more effective than placebo. The multi-faceted adverse effects of antidepressants include emotional blunting, sexual dysfunction, a number of physical ailments and chronicity in the course of depression. These adverse effects are often not easy to identify as stemming from the medication and may be mistakenly attributed to the patient's own emotional difficulties. This presents a challenge to the process of psychotherapy with the risk of creating an impasse and unfavourable outcome. In most cases, a gradual process of withdrawal from antidepressant medication is necessary to reduce the impact of these side effects both on the patient's quality of life and on the psychotherapy process. A clinical case of a patient with a 10-year history of psychiatric medication and hospitalisations, who was suffering from medication stressful adverse effects while not improving psychiatrically. A gradual withdrawal of psychiatric medication coupled with a combination of supportive and exploratory psychotherapy led to a more favourable prognosis and clear improvements in the patient's life.

ANGER, RAGE, RACE, WHITE GAZE, PSYCHOANALYSIS, FANON, BLACK, RACISM

The 2020 Black Lives Matter (BLM) protests were a stark reminder of the reality of problematic ‘race’ relations. This paper, originally conceived in the aftermath of George Floyd's murder with his final words ‘I can’t breathe!’, examines the psychoanalysis of anti-black racism as a contemporary problem to address. This raises important epistemological questions about the forms of knowledge that get produced given the complex relationship between psychoanalysis and coloniality. Frantz Fanon unpacked the impact of racial violence and the white gaze as one of alienation, nonbeing and Black Rage in White Skin, Black Masks. This paper makes use of Fanon's 1952 thesis and clinical vignettes from analysts of colour in relation to ‘race’ as well as secondary literature on psychoanalysis and postcoloniality inviting the reader to appreciate Black Rage as a legitimate and constructive affect. I submit two ‘anchors’ for psychoanalysis to consider in theory and in practice for the birth of a physical and psychic ‘room to breathe’, a place for the black individual to exist with more psychological sovereignty: (1) an extension of Melanie Klein's depressive position and (2) an extension of the concept of mourning, as crucial intrapsychic processes for black lives to matter. The argument advanced is that, due to the extraordinary historical, social and political circumstance placed on black people as a racially oppressed group, the trauma of racism is one of alienation to a zone of nonbeing, a ‘space’ which, incidentally, offers radical hope in the form of Black Rage. Psychoanalysis is adequately positioned to acknowledge Black Rage as a powerful affect and civic tool, and this may be thought about through intrapsychic processes originating in classical psychoanalytic theory as well as Kleinian object relations, principally the concepts of mourning and depressive awareness, which considered together liberate aspects of therapeutic work.

CHRONIC SUICIDALITY, PSYCHOTHERAPEUTIC TREATMENT, PSYCHOTHERAPY

People who seriously consider killing themselves over a protracted period of time, usually years, represent great treatment challenges. Chronic suicidal ideation represents a communication of conscious and unconscious wishes that may be clarified through psychotherapy leading to various outcomes. For one group of patients, this focus will eventually change as they move gradually, over long periods of time, towards more life-affirming goals; a second group will continue to think intensely about suicide for many years, despite various psychotherapeutic interventions, without resorting to self-destructive action; and a third group will go on to attempt suicide which may or may not end in death. In this paper, we present two case studies describing the treatment of patients struggling with chronic suicidality who engaged in psychotherapy but with different outcomes. We discuss the possible outcomes and consider influential factors and suggestions for therapeutic interventions.

In this edition, Focus Point features three articles reflecting some of the diversity of opinion that exists around the issue of gender identity, a diversity which is also reflected elsewhere in this edition and in other articles in recent editions. As a sociologist, Finn Mackay's article provides a perspective from outside the field of psychoanalytic and Jungian thinking and practice. Mackay draws our focus to the gendered culture in which we live, questions whose lives and what is under scrutiny and argues for a reconsidered discussion on gender, informed by more awareness of that context. Wayne Full, Director of Academic and Strategic Development at the British Psychotherapy Foundation, presents research findings related to being transgender and issues of gender identities. His interviews with psychoanalytic, psychodynamic and Jungian practitioners provide detailed information and insight into some of the range of views, concerns and reflections of clinicians working currently. Psychoanalytic psychotherapist Susan Evans draws on her clinical experience working with adults, children and families with gender identity issues in an account of the complexities of such work. Highlighting recent legal and policy developments, Evans questions the appropriateness of medicalised approaches and advocates for a cautious, holistic framework, including a thorough psychological assessment, in addressing gender dysphoria.

GENDER, TRANS, FEMINISM, QUEER, GENDER IDENTITY

This article will argue that there is no war on gender, in the context of the so-called ‘gender wars’. The dominant binary model of gender as male, masculine, heterosexual or female, feminine, heterosexual is not under scrutiny. There is an old and ongoing attempt to control sex, gender and sexuality and constrain and construct what these mean for the benefit of the patriarchal status quo. GENDER DYSPHORIA, TRANSGENDER, DETRANSITION, AUTISM, HOMOSEXUAL, PUBERTY BLOCKERS, AFFIRMATION, CASS REVIEW

The increasing prevalence of gender dysphoria or transgender identity in children and adolescents has raised clinical, ethical and psychological concerns, particularly regarding the efficacy and appropriateness of medical interventions. This paper explores the critical role of thorough psychological assessment in addressing gender dysphoria, with a focus on the closure of the Tavistock NHS Gender Identity Service (GIDS) and the findings of the Cass Review. The author draws on her clinical experience to argue for a comprehensive, individualized approach to the treatment of children and young adults with gender identity conflicts. Key issues discussed include the lack of a robust evidence base for early medical treatments, such as puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones, and the ethical implications of medicalising the bodies of children before psychological and physical maturity. The paper argues that many children presenting with gender confusion may be navigating complex psychological conflicts, including issues of identity, sexual orientation, anxiety and trauma, and that rushing into potentially harmful and life-changing medical treatments may remove opportunities for addressing these emotional struggles. The author critiques the affirmative model of treatment, advocating for a more cautious, holistic and empathetic framework that prioritises improved assessment, psychological support and the time required between early adolescent pubertal changes and full sexual, psychological maturation. The paper highlights the implications of the Bell v. Tavistock Judicial Review and questions the issue of informed consent to hormone treatments. The author calls for the restoration of ethical clinical practices aiming to reduce potential harm and improve long-term outcomes.

Juliet Newbigin  

Karl Figlio's book is exactly what the title describes. It is a closely argued account of a revised psychoanalytic theory of masculinity, written from a Kleinian perspective. He has been working on these ideas for some time, in a book called Psychoanalysis, Science and Masculinity (2000), and a 2010 paper, Phallic and Seminal Masculinity. Here he explains more fully what he means by the term “seminal”, his particularly innovative contribution to the subject.

Freud's “surprising discovery” of the pre-Oedipal dimension of early experience—“like the discovery…of the Minoan-Mycenaean civilization behind the civilization of Greece” (Freud 1931 p.226)—led to his rethinking of female development in his late papers, Female Sexuality (1931) and On Femininity (1933), and provoked outcry among some women analysts in the psychoanalytic community. In the third of the Three Essays on the History of Sexuality, “The Transformations of Puberty”, published in 1905, he had claimed that before puberty the girl was “anaesthetic at the vaginal orifice” and was exclusively interested in clitoridal masturbation, believing her clitoris the equivalent of the boy's penis. This reflected his assumption of “phallic monism”—that for small boys and girls, there is only one genital—the penis—and that both sexes start life believing that they have it. It was the discovery of the anatomical distinction between the sexes that ushered in castration anxiety for the boy, and the traumatic realisation of her lack for a girl (Freud, 1925). In the papers he wrote later, he described femininity as a “riddle”, and how a woman was not born feminine, but somehow “comes into being”, developing “out of a child with a bisexual disposition” who has to learn to inhibit her aggressive impulses and adapt herself to the ‘receptive’ and ‘passive’ social roles for which she is destined (Freud 1933 pp. 116-118). Figlio quotes Karen Horney in particular, who argued strongly against Freud's claim that the girl was ignorant of her vagina and its reproductive function, valuing only her clitoris. Horney denied the existence of a phallic stage of development in girls, claiming instead that the phallic stage in boys was partly a defence against the threat of ‘feminisation’ from the mother's influence. Horney, Helena Deutsch and Melanie Klein all insisted that the girl was aware of the reproductive capacity of her body from childhood. In reaction against Freud's insistence on the primacy of the phallus, they argued that the interiority of the woman's sexual anatomy structured a woman's subjective experience and the anxieties it gave rise to, in a way that was different from those of a man (see Breen, 1993).

Through teaching and speaking on sexual and gender diversity in psychoanalysis over the years, I have come to observe a feature of how discussions on these topics often unfold. First, the persistence of prejudicial norms against trans and queer people in our profession is recognised. Then a careful case is made for reconceptualising metapsychological precepts that veil these damaging attitudes by codifying them in rarefied abstractions. Of greatest urgency in this regard is, of course, deconstructing the cardinal myth of psychoanalysis, the Oedipus Complex. As a purportedly universal account of kinship, Oedipal theory reduces the polyvocality of gender and sexuality to an ahistorical and acultural binary, thereby simultaneously normalising and transcendentalising their dichotomisation. Once this sort of case has been made, a plea to urgently revise the sorts of harmful, entrenched, therapeutic techniques derivative of such metapsychological precepts is submitted. For example, the Kleinian imperative, advanced amongst others by Hanna Segal, to interpret a patient's homosexuality as an unconscious attack on their parents because non-normative sexualities are inescapably perverse, narcissistic and indicative of developmental arrest (Segal & Abel-Hirsch, 2007, p. 253).

At this point, a participant almost invariably interjects: ‘Hold on everybody. Can we just pause to think for a minute?’ Notable about such interpolations is less their imperious elision of the rich thinking prior to the intervention, although that is, of course, significant. It is, rather, more that their seemingly unimpeachable call to ‘pause for thought’ is, in fact, a forceful demand for the opposite, namely, that thinking stop. Immediately. That thinking has gone dangerously too far already, and it is nigh on time to revert to the comforting certainty and reassuring familiarity, of received opinion and accepted bias.

I mention this because it bears directly upon the story of Saketopolou's and Pellegrini's Gender Without Identity, the publication history of which is a veritable return of the repressed, a triumph over formidable institutional attempts at censorship and suppression. DEATH DRIVE, LIFE DRIVE, NARCISSISM, NEGATIVE PACT, NEGATIVE WORK, SICK CHILD

In this article, I examine the work of the negative, in particular denial, through the case of a sick child and his family, and its transformations. A child's serious illness mobilizes the family group in particular to deny, in a collusive manner, breakdown and death anxieties. I hypothesize that Emile's serious illness shifted the family alliance from a narcissistic contract to a negative pact. However, according to several authors, the negative has a double significance and can be structuring. I will show how therapy and playing with this child encouraged the emergence of greater symbolization and the elaboration of the Oedipus complex, or how to move from a devastating, disorganising negative, a pure product of the death drive, to a structuring negative, where life drives and death drives become entangled. The analyst's investment in the child's psychic life allows the objectalising function to unfold, which, as this therapy shows, involves taking the sexual function into account. Narcissistic issues are also dealt with, in an intricate way.

CHILDHOOD ADVERSE EXPERIENCES, PERSONALITY ORGANIZATION, PSYCHACHE, SUICIDAL THOUGHTS

This study examined the relationships between adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and personality organization with suicidal thoughts through the mediating role of psychache using structural equation modeling (SEM). A total of 200 adult outpatients with mental disorders were included in the descriptive cross-sectional study using the purposive sampling method based on self-referral. The data were collected using the Beck Scale for Suicidal Ideation (BSSI), Adverse Childhood Experience International Questionnaire (ACE-IQ), Inventory of Personality Organization (IPO) and Orbach and Mikulincer Mental Pain Scale (OMMP). The results indicated that ACEs, personality organization and psychache explained 72.3% of variations in suicidal thoughts. ACEs, personality organization and psychache have significant positive direct associations with suicidal thoughts. ACEs and personality organization have significantly positive indirect connections to suicidal thoughts through the mediating role of psychache. This study has shown a fitted SEM for the direct and indirect relationships of ACEs and personality organization with suicidal thoughts concerning the mediating role of psychache. These results have implications for the development of psychodynamic interventions and community-based initiatives for individuals dealing with suicidal thoughts.

This paper examines epistemological plurality in contemporary relational psychoanalysis. I draw on clinical material with my own clients who have experienced environmental trauma in early life, such as experiences of incest, battery, abuse and molestation. In this paper, I put forward arguments for the positivist thinking within the development of psychoanalysis, as well as drawing on neuroepistemology, postmodernism and hermeneutic philosophy to consider the ways in which epistemological plurality may provide a more holistic way of conceptualising clients concerns. In this paper, I highlight the role that language, and the analysis of language, plays in meaning making within psychotherapy.

This paper underscores the dual responsibility in psychoanalytic practice: addressing individual and societal traumas. Using Benjamin, a third-generation Holocaust survivor, as a case study, it advocates integrating societal traumas into psychoanalysis, moving beyond individual denial. Benjamin's journey, involving psychoanalysis and community support, highlights the importance of active engagement with trauma for post-memorial healing. The psychotherapist, in this case, plays a crucial role in witnessing and addressing intergenerationally transmitted trauma, fostering the patient's transformation and confronting their own historical connections to broader societal traumas.

ANALYTIC FIELD, COLLECTIVE TRAUMA, OVERLAPPING REALITIES, SHARED TRAUMA, SHARED TRAUMATIC REALITY, TRAUMA

Collective traumatic events such as hurricanes, wars and pandemics result in a series of devastating consequences for entire communities, not only in material terms, but also psychologically, politically and culturally. As the psychotherapist/psychoanalyst and patient are part of the same social group, it is understood that when faced with a misfortune of such magnitude both will be affected by its impact. This phenomenon is called shared trauma, an extraordinary, inevitable and multifaceted situation that will cross the intersubjective clinical scenario, mobilising feelings in the analytic pair and calling on the professional to rethink his practice. This article discusses the possible implications of shared trauma for the analytic field and suggests some ways of dealing with such situations. To construct this writing, a bibliographical review was carried out on trauma, shared trauma and the analytic field in psychoanalysis. Furthermore, some vignettes that were taken from semi-structured interviews with psychoanalysts who worked during the covid-19 pandemic will be presented to illustrate this study. Pubmed, Embase, PsycInfo, Scopus and VHL platforms served as search sources. Even though not all publications used in this research were based on psychoanalytic theory and experience, they contributed significantly. Through this investigation, we raise the hypothesis that working with psychoanalysis, more than an occupation, holds a structuring function that protects the psyche of its professionals.

Introduction

Just over two centuries ago, the English physicist Sir David Brewster patented an invention he called the kaleidoscope, a toy in which coloured pieces of glass reflected repeatedly in three mirrors creating a pattern. In order for this to be symmetrical and for the reflections not to overlap, the mirrors had to be positioned with the edges of the correct triangular prism, forming angles of a certain value.

A century and a half later, on the other side of the Channel, the French analyst Jacques Lacan suggested that normal mental functioning requires a structuring object that binds together the symbolic (language), the imaginary (fantasy) and the real (unsymbolised). Without this defined ‘value’, the Name-of-the-Father, a person is left with a gap which is then filled with psychotic elements such as delusions and hallucinations.

This issue of Clinical Commentaries using these ideas attempts to give a definite shape to the split and projected part of psyche. Its configuration is determined not only by the theoretical refractions of the commentators, but also by their paradigms—the adult, child–parent and couple analytic perspectives. The combination of these different reflections is like the mirrors of a kaleidoscope (Bion's alpha function), allowing the fragmented parts of the psychotic world to be assembled into a more coherent, thinkable picture in the minds of the readers and perhaps similar patients.

I would like to thank the three commentators who generously shared their insights, and the colleague who kindly provided the clinical material.

Brett Kahr

Brett Kahr  

Many years ago, I worked regularly with extremely physically and intellectually disabled patients, most of whom simply could not travel to my consulting room by 316 themselves and thus had to be accompanied by nursing assistants or by professional carers. Likewise, I treated numerous forensic patients, including many convicted felons, all of whom would be transported to my office by social workers or by probation officers. In each of these instances, the escorts would always remain tucked away in the waiting room while the patient and I would meet in my consulting room for our regular 50-minute sessions.

By contrast, distressed couples undergoing marital psychotherapy will never arrive at the office with nursing assistants or social workers. Indeed, both partners in a couple relationship will generally enter the office simultaneously and will embark upon treatment together.

Thus, when I discovered that the patient ‘Becky’—a seemingly competent and physically capable adult—would require her husband ‘Ike’ to accompany her to the psychotherapist's office and to seat himself in the waiting room, I found this an extremely unusual episode. Ike did, on at least one occasion, join Becky for a session, as readers will know, but, for the most part, he remained outside of the office. Thus, one must wonder whether Becky and Ike engaged in this unique style of arrival as a secret, unconscious wish to immerse themselves in proper couple psychoanalysis, or whether both partners actually knew that Becky suffered more extensively from psychotic or borderline illness and that, rather like a disabled patient or a convicted forensic patient, she really did require a nursing husband who would care for her in this unusual fashion.

Having now absorbed this well-written clinical commentary at least 10 times, endeavouring to comprehend this rich and complex material as well as possible, I have developed the hypothesis that, in spite of Becky's seemingly sturdy capacities as a woman who managed to forge a marriage and to give birth to children, and, not least, to display huge empathy, speaking kindly to the psychotherapist when he or she sneezed in session, one cannot help but wonder whether Becky has truly suffered from what I have come to refer to over the years as ‘psychological infanticide’ (Kahr, 1993, p. 269), namely, the devastating trauma of enduring early parental death wishes (cf. Kahr, 1993, 2007a, 2007b, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2025).

Barry Richards

Poole, UK

Barry Richards  

Judith Butler has, since the publication in 1994 of the book Gender Troubles, been one of the most cited intellectual sources of the ferment around ‘trans’, and in debates concerning sexuality and gender more widely. That book established Butler as a leading figure in ‘queer studies’, whose theory of gender as ‘performative’, not an essence, has become a major reference point in academic debate. This latest book is not easy reading in parts. Butler the philosopher sometimes makes use of extended logical sequences (a entails b, and in turn c must follow from that…) to make a point. This measured and abstract style, while heavy going at times, differs from the clamour of much public discourse in the area of ‘gender’—in the peculiar sense, attached by Butler to the single word, of politics around gender issues. ‘Gender’ is the broad collection of issues and demands which along with race and decolonisation are at the centre of today's culture wars: the agendas of lesbian, gay and queer activisms, anti-heteronormativity, different family structures, access to abortion and reproductive technologies, and the rights of ‘trans’ and other emergent sexual minorities.

But despite its often scholarly manner, this is an intemperate and divisive book. Its apparent cogency is overshadowed by its assertions of how dark forces of fascistic totalitarianism have created globally an image of gender politics as a destructive threat, which they then use to spread fear and to incite support for their own life-destroying ends. Obviously hateful attacks on people associated in different ways with different ‘gender’ issues do occur and vary in different contexts in their motives (conscious and unconscious) and consequences. However, book's aim appears to be to roll up all forms of opposition to what Butler sees as a unified ‘slate’ of positions on the different issues and to represent all those forms, whether hatefully violent or peacefully civil, as different facets of the same repressive force. This creates an image of a unified and destructive phenomenon, a mirror to the imagined threat which, it is claimed, others have fabricated around gender. And, like the authoritarian voices which Butler rightly criticises for their repressiveness towards diversity, the massified image of an omnipresent and ultimately ‘fascist’ threat risks encouraging split and absolute states of mind, this time amongst the supporters and sympathisers of ‘gender’ politics.

Joanne Brooks  

In this timely, practical and much needed book, Alessandra Lemma develops an argument for ethical self-discipline in psychoanalytic practice. First Principles reexamines ethical theories in the light of psychoanalytic clinical practice and in the spirit of suspending knowledge and certainty. It is written for psychoanalytic colleagues in general, whatever frequency or length of analytic work they practice.

In this book, Lemma proposes that to advance clinical practice, we need a rigorously applied ethical theory to help us make ethically informed choices in the field of psychoanalysis. Lemma argues that psychoanalysis has not given enough attention to ethics other than a passing nod or reference in clinical papers or training courses. Yet, she argues, the clinician is constantly having to process issues of an ethical nature in their work, just as they have to do in their lives.

The book is divided into two parts, the first a theoretical deep dive into the ethical scene with a specific focus on the field of applied ethics and bioethics. This provides the context for the second half of the book where she examines how such an ethical framework can be learnt and applied clinically by adopting some key principles, and here she helpfully gives some interesting ethically complex clinical examples.

Lemma sets the scene in the introductory chapter with an aptly chosen quote from Rilke's collection Letters to a Young Poet (1929). “‘…be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and to try to love the questions themselves like locked rooms, like books written in a foreign language.…’ “(p. xi). She writes, ‘I draw your attention to Rilke's quote because I want to invite you, the reader, to love and live the questions as you read this book.’ This becomes something of a leitmotif throughout her entire thesis. And just as the young poet turned to Rilke for help on being a poet and how to live well, we the reader are treated to Lemma's knowledge and experience of psychoanalysis and ethics as she shows us how constantly reflecting on what we are doing and why, and asking difficult questions of ourselves in relation to our work, can help create a principled internal space, a ‘space in the therapist's mind that acts as an inner applied ethicist in relation to the therapist's own practice’ (p. 24) or, what she terms an ‘ethical chóros’.

Tom Wooldridge sets himself an ambitious task for this slim volume, part of Routeldge's series of Contemporary Introductions. He hopes it will serve as an introduction to psychoanalytic thinking for clinicians already working in the field of Eating Disorders, as well as providing an overview of the contemporary understanding of this patient group for those familiar with psychoanalytic ideas, students and more general readers. It is a sign of his considerable skill as a writer but foremost as a conceptualiser of the inner world of patients suffering from eating disorders that he achieves all of this and more.

The book aims to consolidate the important accumulation of thinking about eating disorders that the psychoanalytic community has contributed over many decades. Treatment of mental health conditions with such high mortality rates as eating disorders have (understandably) emphasised interventions focused on symptom reduction and management. Wooldridge hopes in this book to draw our attention to the underlying psychological difficulties which may remain, even if the patient experiences a full recovery from the eating-related symptoms following treatment.

I was asked to review this book in my capacity as a trainee psychodynamic psychotherapist whose MA dissertation was in the area of eating disorders. This involved conducting a literature review of psychodynamic writing on the subject of anorexia, where I came across Wooldridge's previous overview of this area: ‘Psychoanalytic Treatment of Eating Disorders: When Words Fail and Bodies Speak’ (Routledge, 2018). That volume provided a much-needed bringing together of contemporary psychoanalytic thinking on disordered eating, including contributions from Kathryn J. Zerbe, Danielle Novack and others. It also contains a chapter by Wooldridge himself on pro-anorexia Internet forums, some of which is repurposed in the excellent final chapter of this volume. Whilst that collection gained breadth from its array of contributors, Wooldridge's new volume gains focus and coherence from having Wooldridge as the sole author.

My colleague and friend, the psychotherapist, author and campaigner Paul Gordon, has died aged 70. While eschewing the limelight, Gordon was an influential and unique voice in the world of contemporary psychotherapy. Author of over 10 books, and multiple articles, he was for many years Chair of the Philadelphia Association, originally founded by the brilliant if mercurial R.D. Laing.

He wrote a number of papers in the BJP, perhaps most notably in the early days about race and psychoanalysis, such as Souls in Armour: Thoughts on psychoanalysis and Racism (Gordon, 1993a) and Keeping Therapy White (Gordon, 1993b), as well as works linking psychotherapy and the arts such as The Celluloid Couch: Representations of Psychotherapy in Cinema (Gordon, 1994).

The papers about race and politics were part of his transition from a more campaigning early adulthood into a socially informed psychotherapy. Born in Glasgow in 1954 to Stanley Gordon, businessman, and Wilma Donaldson, speech and play therapist at psychoanalytically informed Notre Dame Child Guidance Clinic, Paul attended St. Aloysius College and then studied jurisprudence at Glasgow University. He then worked at the Scottish Council for Civil Liberties where he organized the first Scottish Conference on Children's Rights in 1978, and remarkably took the case that ended corporal punishment in Scottish schools to the European Court of Human Rights, ending the use of the dreaded tawse (leather belt).

In 1980, Paul moved to London to work for the Runnymede Trust, where his prolific campaigning and writing, including at least six books, focused mostly on racism, discrimination and social policy. Some of his more important pre-therapy writings included White Law: Racism in the Policy, Courts and Prisons (Gordon, 1983) and New Right, New Racism (Gordon & Klug, 1987), and in 1992, along with Yasmin Alibhai Brown, he gave the Annual Lecture for the Race Relations, entitled Race Equality in Europe: Problems and Potential.

His political commitment and determination to improve people's lives led him to train as a psychotherapist at the Institute of Psychotherapy and Social Studies, and later at the Philadelphia Association. It was at the Philadelphia Association that he really came into his own and developed his philosophy. His first major work there was Face to Face (Gordon, 1999) in which he outlined a model of therapy deeply rooted in philosophy and literature from Merleau-Ponty to Husserl and Emanuel Levinas. While taking seriously the importance of the external world, he made a case for how authentic human presence and conversation could be transformative. The following papers were presented at the annual Cassel Summer Conference in June 2024, which was entitled ‘Relationships with Reality—Working with Self-Harm, Dissociation and Trauma in Individuals and Institutions’. The conference was hosted by Clinical Lead Dr Kimberley Barlow and Inpatient Lead Dr Miriam Barrett who welcomed professionals, patients and ex-patients to a marquee in the beautiful Cassel gardens where guests enjoyed a delicious lunch alongside these three equally nourishing papers. The authors are a Psychotherapist, a Psychiatrist and two Psychosocial Nurses from the Cassel team.

The Cassel Hospital's inpatient programme is a National Specialist Tier 4 Personality Disorder Service for adults who are in a state of crisis or breakdown resulting from a complex interplay of severe mental health problems, longstanding deprivation, abuse and neglect. It is unique in offering a highly specialised combination of formal psychoanalytic psychotherapy and psychosocial nursing in a therapeutic community setting.

Patients come to the Cassel often having exhausted every other method of treatment. Throughout their 9-month-long stay, patients are expected to play an active role in supporting, challenging—and having fun with!—other patients, and in the general maintenance of their temporary home. As in other shared living spaces, there are rotas for cooking, shopping, cleaning, chairing meetings, looking after visitors and so on. Psychosocial nurses aim to get alongside patients as they tackle these ordinary tasks, offering themselves as emotionally alive sounding boards for the often not at all ordinary feelings they can stir up and the (self-)destructive behaviours which can follow.

The unconscious dynamics underlying patients' difficulties are worked on in a psychotherapy group as well as in individual psychoanalytic psychotherapy sessions, each of these twice weekly. We aim for an overarching culture of enquiry by attending to the kind of splitting that is a hallmark of our patients' attempts to manage their difficulties, and to the containment of the institution as a whole.

SELF-HARM, SELF-INJURY, COUNTERTRANSFERENCE, INTERPERSONAL PROCESSES, PERSONALITY DISORDER, REFLECTIVE PRACTICE

Self-harm is common and familiar to many healthcare professionals working in mental health and emergency medicine. Encounters with patients who have self-harmed frequently elicit powerful emotional responses from professionals, which have been explored and characterised in a number of existing qualitative studies. Self-harm serves a number of different functions, ranging from conscious, intrapsychic motivations such as affect regulation, to interpersonal communicative functions which are understood within the psychoanalytic literature to be largely unconscious. This paper aims to explore the unconscious communicative functions of self-harm by characterising the common emotional responses of healthcare professionals encountering patients who have self-harmed, drawing on a narrative review of the existing literature as well as short interviews with clinical staff. Furthermore, this paper aims to understand these responses within the framework of the established unconscious interpersonal functions served by self-harm, thus bridging the divide that can often exist between the front-line exposure to the physicality of self-harm and psychodynamic understanding of the meanings underlying these experiences. The range of responses is organised firstly in terms of the primary emotional reactions, and secondly in terms of the healthcare professional's defences against these emotions, which may themselves be either intrapsychic or enacted. In conclusion, the essential importance of reflective practice in clinical work is emphasised.

Simmi Protab   Currently the Clinical Nurse Manager at the Cassel Inpatient service, in West London NHS Trust. She completed her masters in Psychotherapeutic Approaches in Mental Health with Buckingham New University.
PATIENT AGENCY, PSYCHOSOCIAL NURSING, RELATIONAL PRACTICE, RISK MANAGEMENT, SEPARATION

Risk management in all institutions can become unthinking and process-led, and in this paper we, as psychosocial nurses, have sought to convey how we think about risk at weekends for our patients at the Cassel Hospital. In contrast to many mental health inpatient settings, inpatients at the Cassel go home for the weekend. On one hand, this supports the development of their responsibility for themselves and their social relationships, and on the other, it raises difficulties around separation. These two aspects present us with questions around how to manage risk when patients are not in the hospital. We took as our starting point formal discussions with our inpatient group and nurse team, and linked the ideas that emerged from those discussions with ideas from former members of Cassel staff, drawing on psychoanalytic and psychosocial theories. A dominant theme that emerged was the existence of two selves in the patients' minds – their home self and their Cassel self, and the anxiety shared by patients and nurses about how these two selves can become integrated. Such learning can inform practitioners and policy makers interested in creating services that use relational practice as well as trauma-informed care. These principles could be considered applicable also to health, social care and criminal justice systems.

PSYCHOANALYSIS, LGBTQ+, PSYCHODYNAMIC, HOMOSEXUALITY, MINORITY STRESS, EXPLORATIVE THERAPY, AFFIRMATIVE THERAPY

This paper explores the historical pathologisation of homosexuality and its lasting impact on gay men's mental health and identity, including some of the author's experiences via an autoethnographic narrative. Through the lens of minority stress theory, it examines how societal stigma, internalised shame and structural discrimination contribute to psychological distress among gay men and the broader LGBTQ+ community. The paper critiques the historical complicity of psychoanalysis in reinforcing homophobic narratives while acknowledging contemporary efforts to redress these biases. The paper argues for a therapeutic approach that situates individual distress within broader sociopolitical contexts, advocating for a culturally competent, psychosocially informed psychoanalysis that is both explorative and affirmative, attending to distal (external) as well as proximal (internal) stressors. Finally, it highlights the ongoing struggles within the LGBTQ+ community, urging a collective effort to dismantle intra-community divisions and resist external oppression.

SUPERVISION, CLINICAL MEANING SYSTEM, ABSURDITY, GENERALIZATIONS AND ABSTRACTIONS, METAPHORS, EMBODIED EXPERIENCES

Analytic and philosophical literature suggests that repetitive failures to make sense of internal and external events can seriously undermine our inner meaning systems, leading to feelings of meaninglessness and despair. Accepting the absurdity of the wish for a completely predictable, understandable and manageable world relieves the despair and liberates us from clinging to generalizations and abstractions. It also encourages us to seek personal meanings of our evolving experiences and embrace the life we come to know. These insights are relevant for the supervisory process that helps the supervisee construct an inner clinical meaning system. Repeated failures to understand clinical situations can undermine the supervisee's clinical meaning system, leading to feelings of meaninglessness and despair in their professional life. Accepting the absurdity of wishing for an entirely predictable and understandable therapeutic world can liberate the supervisee from clinging to clinical generalizations and abstractions. It also encourages the supervisee to search for personal and authentic meanings of therapeutic experiences. The supervisor can promote acceptance of this absurdity by highlighting three components of the supervisory materials: metaphorical language, movement and process and embodied experiences.

Meir Peres

Meir Peres

Meir Peres   Clinical Psychologist and Psychoanalyst (member of Israeli Psychoanalytic Society): work in a private clinic, practicing psychoanalytic psychotherapy as well as psychoanalysis. Additionally, work as an instructor in psychoanalytic thought for groups of clinicians and also work as an educator, teaching Freud's technical writings, as well as a broad-comparative course on different schools of psychoanalysis, from Freud onwards, up until today. Since 2016 he is PhD student in Psychoanalysis and Hermeneutics at the Interdisciplinary Department, Bar-Ilan University and involved in Psychoanalytic research concerning unique aspects of the experience which occurs through transference and countertransference in the ‘here and now’ of the therapeutic hour; with the help of the philosophy of language. INTERDISCIPLINARY RESEARCH, NEGATIVE CAPABILITY, BION, KEATS, STAMINA, SUFFERING, AUTHENTIC INNER CONSENT, NEGATIVE SPACE

This paper offers an interdisciplinary approach to negative capability and suffering in the analytic hour. First, I discuss the development that Bion proposes to this concept coined by the poet Keats. Then I analyse the concept's meaning in Keats' poetry, through his poem ‘Ode to a Nightingale’ and propose a unique reading. I show how the poet precedes psychoanalysis in his understanding of mental life, by proposing deep inner authentic consent to accept his suffering while longing for negative capability during the act of creation. Finally, I argue that when attempts to understand the patient through transference and extra-transferential interpretations do not specify his emotional truth, the analyst's consent to bear the feeling of suffering as an attitude while in negative capability in the analytic hour may contribute to the analyst's stamina- therefore to more precise understanding of the patient's emotional truth through the analytic process. I show how this stance parallels that of Keats the poet: the analyst in a negative space of inner authentic consent to suffering – negative capability, communication of projective identification – while dedicating himself to discovering the patient's emotional truth during the analytic hour. The paper is accompanied by vignettes of analysis that demonstrate this idea.

MODERN PSYCHOANALYSIS, PSYCHOANALYTIC TECHNIQUE, SELF-CRITICISM

‘Modern psychoanalysis’ developed by Spotnitz, offers an approach to understanding excessive self-criticism focusing on the role of bottled-up frustration–aggression in its aetiology and proposing treatment aimed at overcoming resistance to the expression of aggression. Modern psychoanalysis purports aetiology to be in the pre-Oedipal period when the infant fails to direct aggressive impulses outwardly. The result is the narcissistic defence in which the person directs aggression towards the self to preserve the object. Treatment is designed to promote the patient's psychological maturation by encouraging the appropriate expression of aggression towards the analyst in the transference, employing techniques such as emotional communication. Familial issues are often a significant contributing factor; reconciliations with an actual bad parent are encouraged in cases in which a constructive emotional interchange is beneficial. Two extended clinical illustrations are presented.

Vera Ramires   Psychoanalytic Psychotherapist of children, adolescents and adults. Professor and researcher at the Graduate Programme in Psychology at Atitus Education, Brazil. Line of research: psychotherapy process and outcomes; psychoanalytic psychopathology; attachment and mentalization; childhood trauma and therapeutic approaches based on mentalization. Dozens of book chapters and articles published in Brazilian and international journals on research in psychodynamic psychotherapy. Published articles in the journals Psychotherapy Research; British Journal of Psychotherapy; Journal of Infant, Child, and Adolescent Psychotherapy; Psychoanalytic Psychology; and Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, among others. ADOLESCENT, COMMUNITY SAMPLES, PSYCHODYNAMIC PSYCHOTHERAPY, RETURN, SYMPTOMATIC CHANGE

The present study aimed to examine adolescents who returned to psychodynamic psychotherapy after terminating a previous psychodynamic treatment and compare them with young people who did not return. We examined the clinical archives of a community-based clinic in Southern Brazil, identifying adolescents who sought psychodynamic psychotherapy after previously terminating a therapy process in the same institution. We carried out statistical analyses investigating the association between variables as well as potential causal relations between them. Age range, symptoms of anxiety/depression, thought problems and the reason for the initial termination were positively associated with returning for a second psychotherapy after the termination of the first one. Rule-breaking symptoms and somatic complaints were negatively associated with returning to therapy. Finally, it was identified that symptoms presented at the beginning of each treatment, such as anxiety/depression, thought problems and aggressive behaviour, were significantly less intense at the beginning of the second treatment. Conversely, somatic symptoms were significantly greater at the second point of referral. Identifying characteristics that may indicate a possible return to treatment can contribute to the optimization of the therapeutic process and facilitate, along with the patient, openness to a new treatment in the future.

Sheila Levi

Sheila Levi   Child-Adolescent-Adult Psychotherapist and Psychoanalyst; Chartered Clinical Psychologist. Works full time in private practice; leads mother-infant observation seminars as well as supervises dissertations at Birkbeck University MSc course for more than 15 years. Until 2015, worked for 15 years as a Highly Specialised Clinical Psychologist in Barnet, Enfield & Haringey MH Trust Tier 3–4 services: in adult services for asylum seekers and refugees and in Learning Difficulties Service as well as in CAMHS with high risk, complex needs adolescents (SAFE) and with neurodevelopmental disorders service (SCAN). Took part and also managed a few applied psychoanalytic community projects in Turkey, Israel and the UK. Her PhD/MPhil dissertation was on empirical testing of Freudian castration anxiety concept through studying the psychological effects of circumcision on Turkish—Muslim boys.
CONCRETE VERSUS SYMBOLIC THINKING, GENDER DYSPHORIA, PRIMARY IDENTITY DEVELOPMENT, PSYCHOANALYSIS, PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS EVASION, SPLITTING OF THE EGO, TRANSGENDERISM

This is an account of my psychoanalytic work with Jozsef, a transgender patient assigned female at birth who ended psychoanalytic treatment abruptly after 1 year. The initial 3 months were three times weekly, then four times weekly for another 9 months. Presenting problems were depression and intense feelings of loneliness. Nothing in the patient's appearance and demeanour, as a 35-year-old man evoked the woman that he had been 10 years earlier. The analysand underwent a double mastectomy but did not dare to undergo genital reconstruction surgery. During his analysis, he described femininity as an illness that he felt the urge to fight off. Following Withers' (2020) framework of multi-level psychological distress evasion, the case illustrates how transgender identification and medical intervention may serve as an attempt to evade profound psychological distress, including attachment trauma and dysregulated affects. Jozsef showed the capacity for mental representation and symbolisation at certain times, but on other occasions, this capacity was lacking. Living with what he had done to his body was less unbearable for him than living with the annihilating suffering resulting from the sense of lacking a primary identity. As his analyst, I believed that the analytic task was to shift the focus from the external concrete reality of the body to bodily fantasies and psychic reality.

David Simpson

david@tdsimpson.com

David Simpson   Training and supervising analyst and past president of the British Psychoanalytic Association and is a fellow of the British Psychoanalytic Society. He was a consultant psychiatrist at the Tavistock Clinic, where he was director for training in child and adolescent psychiatry and led a psychotherapy service for people with learning disabilities and autism. He works in private practice in London. He has written on a wide range of psychoanalytic topics and has published and presented internationally. He has extensive involvement in providing teaching and training for psychoanalysis in Eastern Europe.
BION, CURIOSITY, EMOTIONAL GROWTH, LINK, LOVE, MOTHERING INSTINCT, PATERNAL FUNCTION

In this paper the author explores the emerging model of maternal care which Bion uses to understand analytic function and attitude. Inspired by Bion, he suggests that both curiosity and love are important for mothering capacity in nurturing emotional growth, both in childcare and in analytic work. In his view, of central importance in both of these is the strength of the links to the father or paternal figure. He considers that Bion struggled with a problem in his earlier analytic work, illustrated in his paper ‘On Arrogance’, that followed his prioritisation of curiosity, of seeking knowledge, over its emotional impact. The author suggests that Bion's later change towards a focus on the growth of Being (O), and his recommendations regarding the analyst's attitude, namely a disciplined suspension of memory and desire during psychoanalytic sessions, were aimed at addressing this problem, bringing Bion into line with Klein and Freud.

Jaime Yasky   Clinical psychologist, psychotherapist and supervisor with training in psychoanalytic psychotherapy, working at the Child and Youth Mental Health Service, in private practice, and teaches at the Master of Mental Health at the University of Queensland, and the Brisbane Centre for Psychoanalytic Studies. He has a particular interest psychosomatics, and developed a PhD project on resistance to psychoanalytic treatment among patients with somatic disorders. He has published articles in Spanish and English on psychoanalytic practice and about research on the treatment of patients with somatic disorders.
CONVERSION SYMPTOMS, SOMATIC SYMPTOMS, PSYCHOSOMATICS, PSYCHOANALYSIS, SYMBOLISATION, PSYCHOTHERAPY

Initially, Freud proposed two distinctive ways of understanding somatic symptoms: the hysterical conversion and the actual neuroses models. The original conversion model posited that somatic symptoms had meaning and resulted from psychic mechanisms, whereas actual neuroses model proposed somatic symptoms had no meaning and resulted from physiological rather than psychic processes. Psychoanalytic psychosomatics has evolved much since those initial postulates. Insufficiencies in psychic processing of emotional experience has become a key problem for the understanding of somatic symptoms, and consequently supporting psychic processing has become the main technical challenge. Starting from Freud, this paper explores the evolution of explanatory models and technical approaches for the treatment of people affected by so-called ‘psychosomatic’ pathology. Some technical implications of these developments are discussed in relation to a case example.

Timothy Keogh   Training and supervising analyst with the Australian Psychoanalytical Society (APAS) and an Adjunct Associate Professor at the University of Sydney. He is a past President of APAS, the founding President of the Australian Forensic Psychotherapy Association (AFPA), current Chair of the Scientific Committee of the International Psychoanalytical Association (IPA), as well as Co-Chair of its Couple and Family Psychoanalysis committee (COFAP) and a member of its Violence Committee. He is also the President of Penthos Inc, a psychoanalytic charity providing a free brief intervention for parents experiencing prolonged grief. He has authored numerous articles on individual, couple and forensic psychotherapy and has written and co-edited several books, including The Internal World of the Juvenile Sex Offender: Through a Glass Darkly then Face to Face.
PRIMITIVE MENTAL STATES, PRIMARY NARCISSISM, UNDIFFERENTIATED OBJECT, VIOLENCE, SOMATIC COUNTERTRANSFERENCE

Originally psychoanalytic understandings concerning the capacity to tolerate otherness were linked to the concept of narcissism. Freud (1914) had originally identified a protective stage of ‘objectless’ primary narcissism in normal development and a secondary narcissism, which involves a withdrawal of attachment to the external object. Recent theoretical understandings have identified very early stages of development, known as primitive mental states, wherein the other is both poorly differentiated and psychically represented, leading to unique anxieties and defences. I wish to demonstrate how in working with such states of mind associated violent exigencies can emerge, which if not identified and carefully managed, can stymie psychic growth. In managing such exigencies, it is proposed that the therapist needs to be available to the patient as what Bick has termed a ‘complex undifferentiated object’. This leads to a way of navigating the point at which the patient can suddenly switch from a desperate need for such an object, to a fear of being annihilated by it. In this process, the value of identifying primitive anxieties through one's somatic countertransference experiences is highlighted, as is the utility of a continuum of developmental anxieties, initially proposed by Ogden (1989), which can be used as a therapeutic compass in such a clinical landscape. Two case vignettes are presented which demonstrate how the presence of the therapist moved from being imperative to the patient's survival to being potentially annihilating, and how this was worked with to facilitate psychic growth.

Mark Goldblatt MD , Elsa Ronningstam PHD and Reinhard Lindner

Reinhard Lindner

mark_goldblatt@hms.harvard.edu

Reinhard Lindner   Specialist in Psychiatry, Neurology, Psychosomatics and Psychodynamic Psychotherapy (DGPT), full Professor of “Social Therapy” at University Kassel, Institute for Social Work, Head of National Suicide Prevention Programme for Germany (NaSPro). From 1994 to 2012 he was working in the Center for Therapy and Studies of Suicidal Behaviour, University-Hospital Hamburg-Eppendorf, providing short term psychodynamic psychotherapy for acute and chronic suicidal patients, from 2007 to 2018 he worked as consultant for geriatric psychosomatics at the Medical-Geriatric Clinic Albertinen-House, Hamburg and provided a consultation liaison service as well as outpatient (visiting) psychodynamic psychotherapy for very old geriatric patients. His scientific interests are suicidality, suicide prevention, psychotherapy in old age.
COVID-19 PANDEMIC, PSYCHOTHERAPY, REMOTE TREATMENT, SUICIDE

During the worldwide COVID-19 pandemic, important changes were made to the psychotherapeutic process whereby remote treatments became normalised and suicidal distress was communicated from afar. We consider lessons that may be learnt from this experience about the communication of suicidal desperation and engaging the distressed patient through remote mechanisms.

Oedipus and Narcissus: Brothers in Defeat?

Ralph Holtom PHD and Gilly Stiffell MA

Gilly Stiffell

dr.ralph.holtom@gmail.com
https://orcid.org/0009-0005-8037-7100

Gilly Stiffell   Psychoanalytic psychotherapist and supervisor in private practice in London and Colchester and a member of FPC and BPC. She has been a training therapist for FPC and CCF. She was a Director of Holtom Associates Ltd, focusing on individual psychotherapy.
OEDIPAL DEFEAT, OEDIPAL TRIUMPH, NARCISSISM, SHAME, SELF-WORTH, DELUSION

This paper looks at those resolutions of the Oedipal situation that are characterised as defeat or triumph. We argue that both are defeats and the situation best resolves when intergenerational rivalry is contained and supportive co-operation is dominant. We are struck by the Narcissistic quality we find especially in triumph and note that Oedipus and Narcissus both lived in a false reality constructed to avoid the shame of their own rejection. We are especially concerned about what happens when the child builds a life based on either defeating or being defeated by the same-sex parent and how this appears and may find resolution in analytic psychotherapy. We consider the situation for the girl as well as for the boy and feel there are important distinctions that warrant further thought. Anonymised clinical material is provided to exemplify how this may play out in life and in our practices.

Dhwani Shah  

‘You will not survive here. You are not a wolf, and this is a land of wolves now’. This chilling declaration, delivered by Benicio Del Toro in Denis Villeneuve's ‘Sicario’ (2015), resonates uncomfortably in our current global climate. We live in a world increasingly defined by hardening boundaries between communities, with a disturbing rise of nationalism, communalism and blatant prejudice and violence towards our fellow humans. Witnessing this increasingly bleak reality, I was heartened to discover a book about how we can find ways of relating and loving across these divides, specifically in the context of intimacy and desire in Hindu–Muslim relationships. Ashis Roy's ‘Intimacy in Alienation: A Psychoanalytic Study of Hindu–Muslim Relationships’ (2024) offers a path forward in relating to and daring to love ‘the other’ that does not succumb to either cynicism or idealization. While tensions and violence between Hindu and Muslim communities continue to escalate in South Asia and beyond, Roy's work courageously examines the psychological underpinnings of romantic intimacy that persists across these divides. Rather than accepting the ‘land of wolves’ as inevitable, Roy explores the contours of the psyche of interreligious romantic couples, offering a rich landscape of psychoanalytic theorizations to understand the complex conflicts, dilemmas and attractions these couples experience.

In his introduction, Roy notes that there has been an erasure of the complexity and mutual influences of Hindu–Muslim relationships. As this complexity of cultural influence is lost, ‘the history of the two communities has become entangled with paranoia and aggression: Hindus and Muslims are being made into true Others of each other’ (Roy, p. 10). Roy courageously asks us to find the ‘Hindu inside the Muslim’ and the ‘Muslim within the Hindu’. Sadly, he notes that in Indian popular imagination today, ‘a Hindu and a Muslim simply cannot be in love’. Multiple layers of mistrust, hatred, and prejudice transform the couple's bond into a forbidden intimacy. One tragic example Roy highlights is the popular racist discourse of ‘love jihad’. This collective Islamophobic myth views all Hindu–Muslim conjugal relationships as coercive and deceitful, portraying Hindu women as victims forced to convert to Islam. This poisonous narrative deploys fantasies of purity and forbidden miscegenation. Against this backdrop, Roy hopes to create a space for Hindu–Muslim couples to give their own voice and meaning to their desires and identities.

Angela Joyce  

This book is an edited collection of papers about the creative and original women who, having been at the heart of what became the Independent tradition within British psychoanalysis, were also crucial in the elaboration of British psychoanalysis 576 more broadly. Perhaps too often the history of the British School is reduced to the dramatic encounters between Melanie Klein and Anna Freud, as though the Independent tradition somehow came out of analysts who did not have or develop a coherent body of thought and clinical practice which could stand up to the kind of scrutiny that was afforded to those two great pioneers. And certainly, the big names associated with the Independent group were largely male—Balint, Winnicott and latterly Bollas, Casement, Parsons amongst others. However, the women who are lauded in this volume each come alive in a series of essays that portray their originality, close attention to their clinical practice and courage to speak out in an institutional atmosphere that has often been antipathetic to their ideas.

The book comes from the collaboration of Elizabeth Wolf (training analyst and Fellow) and Barbie Antonis (Fellow) of the BPAS, who for many years have taught a course about the contribution of independent women as part of the training at the Institute of Psychoanalysis (BPAS). Together they commissioned both seasoned, senior analysts from the BPAS and several of the next generation to contribute to this collection. They are all Fellows or Training Analysts of the BPAS and members of the Association of Independent Psychoanalysts.

The introduction by the co-editors is not only an account of their own creative partnership, but also a description of the anxiety about the atmosphere within which Independent theory and clinical practice was felt to be in danger of fading from view as the BPAS became more dominated by the Klein group. They evoke the sense of a lively engagement on the part of members of the Association to that predicament, moving from an initial beleaguered sense of disquiet at the hostility frequently expressed towards Independent ideas, to a celebration and ownership of that specificity of thought and clinical practice that characterises the tradition. Previously this spawned other publications, including one edited by Williams et al. (2012). In this volume the editors convey an impression of a tradition that is far from fading but very alive in its engagement with ideas that are at the heart of contemporary psychoanalysis. Similarly the contributors to the volume under review bring a hefty degree of scholarship and knowledge of the history of British Psychoanalysis, the Independent tradition and also the broader context. In Jonathan Sklar's account of the significance of the Bloomsbury set and Cambridge for the way psychoanalysis took root in Britain he emphasises the central significance of freedom of thought and resolve against stultifying orthodoxy. Joan Raphael-Leff brings her critical appreciation of the way in which these early women Independent pioneers located the development of mind within relationship, shifting the psychoanalytic account from a largely solipsistic one-person creation to the infant-mother matrix, constituted dyadically, with mind as process evolving through emotional engagement with the caregiver. This had huge consequences for clinical practice where the ‘goal of autonomy was tacitly replaced with a growing belief in lifelong human inter-dependency’ (p. 20). It is largely out of the Independent tradition that the contemporary sensitivity to the analyst's affective response and the countertransference derives, even if it has been taken in different directions.

David M. Black's new book, Psychoanalysis and Ethics: The necessity of perspective (2024), offers a rather timely engagement with the all-important issue of ethics. One might be tempted to respond that ethics is not a new question for psychological consideration—the first ethical code of conduct for the American Psychological Association was promulgated in 1952 already, though it was only in the 70s and 80s hat it rose to deliberate levels of enforcement and integration into training (by contrast, the American Psychoanalytic Association adopted an ethical code of conduct in 1975, followed by sustained debate and controversy over enforcement mechanisms and protocols). There is, though, a difference in the renewed attention to ethics over the last few decades; the concern now seems less with prescribed rules and codes of conduct than with an articulation of the conditions of possibility for ethics in the first place—for the ethical that makes ethics possible. One might credit philosophy, and most notably the work of Emmanuel Levinas (2004, 2013), for this “ethical turn” and its resultant challenge to the human and social sciences for the psychological ontology from which its epistemology and methodological praxis gather form.

Though there are many good, insightful moments in this collection of papers by Australasian psychoanalyst Paul Schimmel, I found it an uneven book. This impression is unfortunately reinforced by some rather sloppy, inconsistent editorship, particularly regarding the way citations are made in the text. The title itself is already something of an oddity: why must the subtitle include ‘of Paul Schimmel’ when his name already appears as the author of the volume?

A poet in his own right, Schimmel begins with a poem about Freud's 39th birthday. He then introduces the book with little more than a listing of the papers in his collection. These appear to have been written over a period of about 20 years but are not presented chronologically. Michaela Chamberlain  

One of the most daunting aspects of undertaking a psychoanalytic psychotherapy training can be the prospect of the ‘infant observation’ component. I remember wondering what it was exactly that I was meant to be ‘observing’ and why. As the mother of three children, I was more than aware of the judgment placed on mothers and how just about everybody had an opinion on what constituted a ‘good’ or ‘bad’ mother. I was concerned that somehow this judgment process had been formalised through an ‘infant observation’, whereby the unconscious worlds of the mother and infant would be determined by the observer in order to diagnose the infant as ‘secure’ or ‘insecure’ through the lens of attachment theory.

Those initial tensions stayed with me throughout my infant observation as I observed the mother and baby (and sometimes father) who kindly allowed me to visit them every week for 2 years. I consider myself extremely fortunate to have shared this time with the family in those precious, vulnerable early months and years, especially as the family I got to know was from a different culture to mine. In addition, for the initial stage of the baby's life, I was often not just with the Mother and baby but in a group with several other mothers and their babies. The mothers would fill the air with laughter and curiosity as they watched their babies (who ranged in age from 3 months to 2 years old) interact with each other. It would be a moment of respite from the sometimes hard work of reverie that required them to try and disentangle their own feelings from those of their babies and make sense of what the babies needed.

It is exactly this interaction between babies that Bradley, Selby and Stapleton so joyously celebrate in their new book, ‘Babies in Groups: Expanding Imaginations’. This extremely accessible book is based on decades of research in infant development, culminating in a fascinating and rigorous research project observing babies being together without adults, initially in triads and then in larger groups.

For a practising clinician to be immersed in historiography, for example quoting the difficult and multilayered writing of Michel De Certeau (1988) is arresting. However, Sanfelipo is not only an analyst with over 20 years of clinical experience, but also the Coordinator for the Centre for the History of Psychoanalysis at the National Library of Argentina. So, his book is a rare thing, a work that is, at one of its focal points, deeply knowledgeable of the internal development of psychoanalysis, yet also mindful of the nuances of broader historical and cultural factors. First published in Spanish in 2018, this new translation makes it available to an English readership for the first time.

The book is organized into five chapters. They refer to progressive chronological periods, which also reflect the deepening of psychological thinking about trauma 591

Was Anna Freud a “Friend of Dorothy”? A Queer Phenomenological Historiography of Anna Freud and Dorothy Burlingham's Personal and Professional Relationship

Harriet Mossop

Harriet Mossop

hm21886@essex.ac.uk

Harriet Mossop   PhD student and Assistant Lecturer in the Department of Psychosocial and Psychoanalytic Studies, at the University of Essex, and Research and Development Officer in the Centre for Anthropological Mental Health Research in Action at the School for Oriental and African Studies, University of London. She is a co-founder of the Queer Encounters research network for psychosocial researchers in gender and sexuality

URL: www.queerencounters.org

, a member of the Queer Analytic Circle, and convener of the ‘Other Women’ reading group for queer women and non-binary people. She has presented papers based on her early research at clinical and academic conferences in the UK.
PSYCHOANALYSIS, QUEER THEORY, ANNA FREUD, PHENOMENOLOGY, HISTORY OF PSYCHOANALYSIS, GENDER AND SEXUALITY

The nature of Anna Freud and Dorothy Burlingham’s 5-decade-long personal and professional relationship has always been subject to speculation. This paper considers the historiography of this important and enigmatic relationship from 1920s Vienna to today. Drawing on Sara Ahmed’s Queer Phenomenology, which theorises sexual orientation and whiteness in spatial terms, I illustrate how the relationship was seen as deviating from the ‘straight lines’ of mid-20th century heteronormative society. I extend this queer phenomenological approach to think about cultural orientations to the relationship through an examination of its depiction in biographies published in the 1980s, the collections at the Freud Museums in London and Vienna, and a fictionalised account of Anna Freud’s life published in 2014. Extending Ahmed’s’ queer phenomenological vocabulary, I identify examples of ‘straightening up’, ‘straightening devices’ and ‘straightening up by queering’. The possibility of finding ‘queer angles’ in Anna Freud’s’ early clinical writings, in contrast to the normative tendencies of her later writing on ego psychology, is explored as a counterbalance to discussions about non-normative sexuality and gender in psychotherapy which typically position these as something new. The relevance for clinical practice today is considered through the lens of an ethical imperative to find space for queer angles in the history of psychoanalysis.

Stephen Morris and Gwion Jones

Gwion Jones

simla6@btinternet.com

Gwion Jones   Member of the Centre for Freudian Analysis and Research and has been practising as a psychoanalyst for over 30 years. He also lectures in the Clinical Psychology Department at Coventry University.
DOMAINS OF IMPLICIT RELATIONAL KNOWING, MOMENTS OF MEETING, GROUP MATRIX

This preliminary study should be regarded as a pilot piece of research designed specifically to explore some of the unconscious dynamics that operate within the Balint Group process. A brief history is offered by introduction, which aims to set this research in the wider context of the influences that shaped Michael Balint's thinking, particularly the view that the primary obstacles in therapeutic work derive from the analyst's own resistances. The study itself attempts to highlight the presence or absence of ‘domains of implicit relational knowing’ between Balint Group participants, within which ‘moments of meeting’ may take place, leading to a change in the thinking/feeling of the Presenter about their case. It is suggested that such domains emerge through unconscious interactions and that the Group Matrix contains and fosters such activity. The rationale for the use of a 7-point scale of participants’ subjective evaluations of feeling attuned/connected or mis-attuned/ unconnected towards the Group, the Presenter and the Conductor is drawn from Attachment/Neuroscience research. The data gathered from two groups, each engaging in two presentations, reveal patterns of identical scores suggesting the presence of ‘domains’, and marked discrepancy scores suggesting their absence. Sufficient ‘domains’ accompanied a change in thinking/feeling for the Presenter, while few ‘domains’ and marked discrepancy scores did not do so. These observations are tentatively discussed with reference to the early origins of unconscious communications.

NEOLIBERALISM, CULTURE OF NARCISSISM, BION'S CONCEPT OF -K, MISREPRESENTATION OF REALITY, MODERN SLAVERY, CULTURE OF ILLUSION

Kazuo Ishiguro’s dystopian novel Never Let Me Go takes place, as the author tells us in ‘England, the late 1990s’ and follows the lives of a group of clones who had been created with the sole purpose of harvesting their organs for transplant. The novel is steeped in an atmosphere of illusion and self-deception while remaining deeply rooted in human emotions. I argue that to some extent it represents all of us, our illusions and self-deceptions. At another level, however, I argue that the novel is a sharp critique of a culture of narcissism and self-interest where human beings are treated as commodities, while creating the illusion that they are special and that ‘they never had it so good’, a saying from another time when self-deception was equally promoted. The paper concentrates on one aspect of this multilayered novel—the misrepresentation of reality and the human wish not to know about painful truths, but instead to create an illusory world. It examines this aspect of the novel in terms of the current neoliberal framework, and the culture of illusion that it promotes by ignoring the violence that underlies it. In particular, it examines how this pervasive aspect of contemporary culture affects the ability of the individual to ask questions and to pursue the truth, what Bion called ‘K.’
