SOCIAL DEFENCES, HEALTH INSTITUTIONS, ELIZABETH MENZIES, WILFRED R, BION

This work consists of an approach to the concept of Social Defences, which consolidates one way of applying psychoanalytic thinking to human institutionality. The author briefly describes the path psychoanalytic theory takes towards the outline of this concept, to emphasise later the implications it has for health institutions. There is a statement about the importance of considering the ways in which individual defences tend to collude with the institutionalized group's unconscious mechanisms, where certain conditions will be determined for the containment of primitive states of mind. Emphasis is made about the possibility that these dynamics have concrete effects on the workers' capacities and health, on the patients' treatment, and mainly on the loss of meaning that these people experience in their link with this institution. Two vignettes are included to attempt an illustration of these dynamics.

AUTISM, DIFFERENCE, DISABILITY, NEURODIVERSITY, NEUROLOGICAL, PSYCHOANALYSIS, PSYCHOANALYTIC PSYCHOTHERAPY

Psychoanalytic psychotherapy and autism have had a complicated relationship. Much of the complication has arisen from patients with autism being misunderstood by those who have used a psychoanalytic lens. These misunderstandings arose not for a lack of trying—but rather from a disavowal of how neurological difference shapes what it means to become a person, and how these differences affect treatment needs. It has been autistic patients who have had to bear the consequences of these misunderstandings in much the same way as they do in their daily lives outside of therapy. It is not the psychoanalytic lens that has failed these patients, but rather its use without reference to the ever-growing body of neurobiological knowledge. In this paper, we make the argument that many of the key psychoanalytic concepts—countertransference, the frame, narcissism, intellectualization and obsessions—need to be reviewed and altered when working with autistic patients.

FERENCZI, FAIRBAIRN, TRAUMA, NARCISSISM, ECHOISM, SOCIAL MEDIA, SELF-HELP CULTURE, NARCISSISTIC ABUSE

The recent explosion of populist narratives around ‘narcissistic abuse’ on social media has prompted millions to seek answers in online self-help communities. Many are advised to enter personal therapy. This paper asks whether consuming such narratives supports or hinders subsequent psychodynamic treatment. To address this, the social media discourses are critiqued through a psychodynamic lens, contrasting them with psychodynamic aims. The author conceptualises patients' relationship difficulties as stemming from internalised traumatic relational patterns. The theories of Fairbairn and Ferenczi are reprised. Case material illustrates the challenges that arise when these patients enter therapy armed with preconceived diagnoses, seeking confirmation of online-informed hypotheses. Those clinging rigidly to simplistic social media narratives often struggle to engage deeply in treatment. The author argues that adherence to reductive formulas should concern psychotherapists given the expansion of social media self-help. It is suggested the field would benefit from psychotherapists publicly addressing the risks of simplistic narratives and highlighting psychodynamic complexity. Modelling nuanced thinking may counteract the confirmation bias patients encounter online.

CLINICAL IMPROVISATION, MOMENTUM AND TRANSFERENCE, NEUROPSYCHOANALYTIC APPROACHES, HOMEOSTATIC CONTEXT, BLACKNESS AS TRANSMISSION

This paper re-evaluates improvisation as a central dynamic in psychoanalytic practice, allowing practitioners to harness momentum and address the states of being ‘stuck’ described by Freud, Jung, Lacan and other analytic thinkers. It takes up Freud's nachträglichkeit, the effects of Derrida's différance, and the affect-focused neuropsychoanalytic approaches cultivated by Solms, Panksepp and others. It proceeds to show how a discourse on sociality developed by Fred Moten and others in the context of Black and performance studies can contribute to psychotherapeutic understanding of the effect of intimacy and the sharing of difference. Interesting connections emerge between an understanding of blackness and an understanding of transference as ‘movement’. Improvisation helps participants in therapy shift between homeostatic balancing and entropic pulls, stimulating emotional flexibility. This paper advocates for psychoanalysis as a social psychotherapy. Clinically, it emphasises the possibilities of fluidity and receptiveness over an emphasis on integration, attachment and individuation.

Paradoxical “Weaning Complex” in Bariatric Surgery: From Hyperphagic Addiction to a Pleasure in Speaking

Pierre Bonny , Charlotte Tazartez and Giorgia Tiscini

Giorgia Tiscini   Professor in clinical psychopathology (Department of psychology, Rennes 2 University, Rennes, Laboratoire de “Recherches en psychopathologie et psychanalyse” - RPpsy); clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst. She works on the links between the subject, the body and the social context, from both a medico-therapeutic and a sociojudicial point of view. She is co-author of “Homeostasis and dyshomeostasis in language and acting out: a dialogue between neurosciences and psychoanalysis” (to be published in 2025 in American Journal of Psychoanalysis), and of “The uncanny crime: the otherness of the crime.” (2023, Rassegna Italiana di Criminologia).
EATING DISORDERS, ADDICTION, BARIATRIC SURGERY, RISK, SUICIDE, UNCONSCIOUS

The aim of this article is to present and discuss the unconscious psychological issues involved in bariatric surgery, in the light of the notion of the “weaning complex”. After highlighting the risk of postoperative suicide, we present the psychic mechanisms of decompensation among the patients concerned. We then recall that hyperphagia leading to obesity is a prevalent form of addiction in consumer societies. We also explore the notion of the “weaning complex” which was developed by Lacan, and show that bariatric surgery is a type of paradoxical and abrupt weaning. Based on the clinical case of a patient suffering from post-operative psychic decompensation and who was previously obese and addicted to food, the article explains that post-operative decompensation results from a major difficulty of shifting the drive satisfaction of food addiction to another object. In conclusion, we argue that restoring a taste for speech to these patients in the context of a clinical encounter is a central issue in countering the exacerbation of the death drive associated with the operation.

d.kaestner@phb.de

Antje Gumz   Professor of Psychosomatics and Psychotherapy and Head of the Master's Program in Psychodynamic Psychotherapy at the Psychological University of Berlin (Psychologische Hochschule Berlin). Her research focuses on psychotherapy and psychotherapy training, particularly therapeutic relationship competencies (e.g., alliance ruptures, interpersonal skills, transference and countertransference, enactments), therapeutic techniques, and mediators of change. She received the Adolf-Ernst-Meyer Prize (2013) and the Heigl Prize (2023) for her empirical work in psychotherapy research. A trained psychoanalyst, psychodynamic and systemic therapist, she also serves as a training analyst and supervisor. Her work is shaped by a strong scientist-practitioner approach, combining clinical expertise with empirical research.
WOUNDED HEALER, THERAPEUTIC ALLIANCE, CHILDHOOD MALTREATMENT, ATTACHMENT, THERAPIST VARIABLES, FACILITATIVE INTERPERSONAL SKILLS

We aimed to investigate (1) if trainee therapists differ from controls regarding childhood maltreatment and adult attachment and (2) if there are associations between childhood maltreatment, adult attachment and the alliance bond capacity. To answer the 1st question, a sample of 134 trainees and psychology students was matched to population-representative controls (CTQ: N = 2504, ECR-S: N = 2555) and compared on the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) and the Experiences in Close Relationships Scale (ECR-S). For the 2nd question, the Facilitative Interpersonal Skills task was used to measure trainees' alliance bond capacity. Regression analysis was performed with age, gender, training status, CTQ and ECR-S scales as potential predictors. We found that psychology students and trainees reported more childhood emotional abuse (t = –6.268; p < 0.001), but less physical neglect (t = 2.927; p = 0.004), a lower tendency to minimize or deny adverse experiences (t = 5.415; p < 0.001) and less attachment avoidance (t = 3.048, p = 0.003) than controls. The alliance bond capacity was predicted by greater therapeutic experience (students vs. trainee, β = –0.284, p = 0.003; with vs. without licence to practise, β = –0.218, p = 0.025) and greater childhood physical abuse (β = 0.200, p = 0.035). Our results emphasize addressing therapists' personal wounds. The potential beneficial effects, suggested by the positive association between physical abuse and alliance bond capacity, require further investigation and replication.

Melanie Williams

m.l.williams@exeter.ac.uk

Melanie Williams   Professor Emerita of Law at the University of Exeter and part-time Lecturer in Law at Aberystwyth University whose research and publication history considers links between law, literature and philosophy. The intersection of these fields with issues of psychological and medical significance led her to qualify more recently as a Psychotherapist.
AGENCY, INJUSTICE, JUSTICE, LACAN, PSYCHOTHERAPY, THERAPEUTIC SPACE

In psychotherapeutic practice, trauma—and its resolution—frequently requires some recognition of the role played by injustice. How and to what extent societies and their legal systems choose to provide formal recognition mechanisms in support of resolving traumas will have a direct impact upon the incidence of mental health, crimes and individual and collective values in the wider community. Trauma associated with the legal system itself, or with broader notions such as ‘social injustice’ may invoke consideration of justice, yet the word ‘injustice’ alone does not appear readily in the lexicon of therapeutic modalities in speaking to the ‘everyday’ experiences emerging in the therapeutic space. So much of client trauma derives from an assault upon personal agency, whether by accident or design, and much recovery involves the restoration of agency by at least calling out the fact of injustice and, through therapy, supporting the empowerment of individuals in determining aspects of their own lives and choices. This paper explores the relevance of the words ‘justice’ and ‘injustice’—especially in their relevance to ‘everyday’ experience—in the therapeutic space.

TRANSPLANTATION, TRANSPLANTATION COMPLEX, THE INTRUDER, SIGNIFICATION, MIRROR OPERATOR, PSYCHOSOMATIC TORUS

Organ transplantation is a complex psychodynamic process. Previous psychoanalytic research has mainly dealt with the psychological integration of the new organ and the conscious and unconscious relationship of the recipient to the transplanted organ and the donor. Some works have also explored organ transplantation from a Lacanian perspective, particularly about the patient (subject) and the transplanted organ (conceptualised as the object a). In the current paper, the processes of signification as well as the integration of the new organ are examined against the Lacanian background of the neurotic, perverse and psychotic structure. An important factor that determines the nature of these structures is the mirror operator. It is a logical operation that mediates between different spaces, for example, in the Lacanian fields, the spaces of the real, the imaginary and the symbolic. The authors discuss the clinical implications for transplant patients and the logical function of the mirror operator in the psychosomatic torus (as a topological model). Jean-Luc Nancy's essay ‘The Intruder’ and the eponymous film by Claire Denis, which dealt with the experience of a heart transplant, are additionally taken into account here.

She obtained her doctorate at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland and is currently a visiting researcher at the Department of Psychology. Her research interest is the intersection of relational psychoanalytic therapy practice and self-determination theory (SDT).
RELATIONAL PSYCHOANALYSIS, DISSOCIATION, MULTIPLICITY OF SELF, ENACTMENT, THERAPEUTIC REGRESSION

This article reviews the conceptualization of mind and therapeutic action in the relational psychoanalytic tradition. It briefly presents the history of relational psychoanalytic thinking that developed from multifaceted clinical experience that both found lacking and challenged classical theory. The review traces relational theory to interpersonal psychoanalysis, which was extended by object relations theory, self-psychology and postmodern epistemology. The paper presents dissociation, multiplicity of self and generative enactments as hallmarks of the relational psychoanalytic tradition. Relational psychoanalysis understands the human mind as composed of horizontally organized self-states. Health is defined as the ability to move flexibly and acceptingly between different self-states, including those that are hated, feared, shamed and even regressive. The denial or avoidance of self-states is conceptualized as dissociative experience, a fertile ground for cumbersome enactments in the therapeutic relationship. As for the implications for therapeutic action, relational theory contends that the therapist's dissociated self-state significantly influences countertransference and can lead to entrenched enactments in the therapeutic process. The article discusses implications of these relational perspectives on both case conceptualization and clinical understanding of the therapeutic situation at hand in different phases of the therapeutic process. The article frequently returns to the work of Winnicott because his work both anticipated the relational turn in psychoanalysis and becomes revitalized in the light of relational theory.

SUPERVISION, METAPHORICAL DIMENSION, REALITY REPRESENTATIONS, DIALOGUE, MUTUAL RECOGNITION

Metaphors, embedded in everyday life, art, literature and the theoretical frameworks of various sciences, shape our interests and influence how we observe, perceive, construct and articulate complex and abstract aspects of reality. Recognizing the metaphorical dimension of our theoretical perspectives prevents us from reifying them—mistaking concepts for direct representations of reality—and from rigidly clinging to our perceptions and beliefs. While analytic therapeutic literature has explored these issues, it has rarely examined them within the supervisory process that focuses on the meanings of therapeutic interactions. Drawing insights from psychoanalytic and philosophical literature, this paper explores the interrelations between recognizing the metaphorical dimension in supervisory theoretical perspectives, adopting a self-critical stance and fostering mutual recognition in the supervisory dialogues. It will be argued that these interconnected elements are essential for achieving the supervisory process's initial and most fundamental goal: making sense of what transpired within the presented therapeutic framework.

In musicology, his research aims to understand aesthetics from an ethical viewpoint, while his inquiry in philosophy, through a meta-ethical lens, addresses the ethical constraints of engaging in philosophical thought. His inclinations in philosophy lean towards existentialism, mysticism, psychoanalysis and irrationalism, whereas in musicology he is drawn to late-Romanticism and aesthetics.
PSYCHOANALYSIS, LOVE, NARCISSISM, SUFISM, JAVAD NURBAKHSH, EGO

This paper critically examines psychoanalysis—particularly ego psychology—by contrasting it with Sufism's approach to the psyche. Drawing on the insights of the Sufi teacher and psychiatrist Javād Nurbakhsh, alongside classical Sufi literature, it argues that the Sufi perspective on the psyche provides insights that challenge the paradigms of ego-based approaches such as ego psychology. In this context, the topics of love and narcissism are explored as prime examples that emphasise a fundamental difference between the Sufi and psychoanalytic models: While psychoanalysis tends to interpret love through the lens of ego-driven and self-referential narcissism, Sufism regards love as a state that overcomes the ego. Without rejecting the notion of love as a self-referential phenomenon, this paper reframes the concept of ‘self-referentiality’, proposing an alternative understanding of it as an egoless state. The aim is to bring to light the advantages of approaches that go beyond ego-centered models of the psyche. Furthermore, the therapeutic implications of the Sufi approach are also explored, particularly regarding the Sufi emphasis on the ‘annihilation of the ego’ as a form of healing.

Introduction

This section of the journal typically features the views of qualified clinicians who have completed their training and become members of a professional society. However, in keeping with the journal's philosophy of providing a platform for diverse viewpoints, all contributors to this issue are candidates.

The concept of candidate is fraught with contradictions. On the one hand, a candidate is not yet a qualified analyst; rather, they are someone undergoing training to be able to perform analytical work subsequently. On the other hand, their training, which includes undergoing analysis themselves and offering analysis to the patients, suggests that they already have the necessary expertize of ‘doing the work and fulfilling the role’ (Marcus, 2021, p. 15).

The etymology of the word also suggests idealistic expectations of candidates—just as an ancient Roman candidatus wore a toga candida when seeking an office by election, candidates are expected to demonstrate a level of soundness and integrity. Perhaps in response to this duality, terms such as analyst in training or affiliate member have increasingly been used instead of candidate in recent years.

The situation facing current candidates is no less contradictory. Compared with their perhaps more fortunate predecessors, they now have to ‘construct the analytic patient’ in conditions where ‘narcissistic Ego Ideal… makes dependence on an object… an unacceptable, humiliating condition’ (Bolognini, 2021, p. 36). Changes in patients' internal structures have become more a reflection of changes in the outside world—the rapid development of digital technologies and social media, the pharmaceutical industry boom, insurance companies, and public healthcare supporting short-term therapies, coupled with the economic downturn, are causing a larger number of modern patients to expect quicker results with less effort.

However, while these changes may introduce new complexities to analytical work, they could also potentially contribute to its development by offering new perspectives (e.g., the emergence of short-term analytical-based therapies, such as Dynamic Interpersonal Therapy and Mentalisation-Based Therapy) and opportunities (for instance, conducting analytic work and training remotely). At the same time, it is important to recognize that this is not universally positive and is the subject of heated theoretical and practical debate.

Introduction

I have often wondered about what it might be like to encounter another clinician's work through the page and then write a clinical commentary based on the words alone. Having been through the process from the other side (as a previous Clinical Commentaries editor), I found myself readily accepting when I was recently offered the opportunity. ‘Gasping for air’ is how I felt when I read about Charlotte, confined to a room with a mother who appeared never to have been able to move forwards in her life after the premature death of her husband, whose own life had been littered by loss. Almost half the material offered is Charlotte's life history and the history of her analysis. There is then a paragraph summary of a Monday session in which we hear no words from the analyst, followed by an excerpt from a Tuesday session. The first words we hear from the analyst are more than halfway through the material provided.

I write ‘the analyst’ but this figure's own identity seems to be in doubt: in the excerpt from Tuesday, they are identified as ‘therapist’. Music accomplishes an unusual feat in his latest book, Womb Life, in that he has created a self-help guide for all pregnant mothers and those who support them, whilst also writing a textbook for any professionals who encounter women in this moment in their lives. One should not be surprised at this, as his previous books all demonstrate his capacity to present complex research evidence and theoretical concepts in accessible and compassionate ways that elucidate and contextualize the topic he addresses. In his ability to synthesize such material into a coherent and moving narrative, I see Music as a pioneer and a trailblazer. In Womb Life, Music holds a delicate line between acknowledgement of the potential impact of adversity on the growing foetus and the need to hold space for parents without blame or shame.

In reading this book I often found Winnicott's famous quotation was in my mind:

There is no such thing as a baby, there is a baby and someone. (1966).

What Music subtly emphasizes throughout is we need to hold in our minds that there is, if all is well, a foetus, a mother, a partner, a support network, and a community. So, many “someones” in an ideal world.

Using psychoanalytic concepts (although rarely naming them as such), neurobiological ideas, attachment theories and other areas of research as well as bringing an intercultural lens throughout, Music writes with his inimitable style of empathy, humour, warmth and generosity. He uses vignettes and quotations from mothers and those who support them to emphasize the complexity in perinatal mental and physical health for mother and foetus.

As a psychoanalyst who works with complex trauma, I have already placed a copy of this book into our service's lending library for patients and see it as a text that provides vital psychoeducation that is such an important aspect of empowerment in trauma-informed care. This is also testament to Music's message intertwined throughout the book that maternal blame, shame, and guilt have no place in this area. I have also recommended the book to many colleagues to deepen our understanding of the concept of early relational trauma and the transgenerational transmission of trauma, which begins before conception and extends in utero and on into birth itself. I am delighted that Music is planning a series of such books, each looking at specific developmental periods.

In this comprehensive book, Melvin compassionately explores the painful reality of being estranged from family members in contemporary society. He offers his personal insights on navigating family estrangement as well as his professional views and expertise derived from his experience as a psychotherapist working in the field of family estrangement.

774

In his book, Melvin portrays estrangement as fundamentally a relationship phenomenon, defined as an act of consciously putting distance (emotional and/or physical) between one or more family members, with a conscious effort to enforce it. Melvin outlines both the emotional and physical types of estrangement in the book as well as the prevalence of family estrangement in modern society. He provides an overview of what he has discovered about the topic, his learning about how families become estranged and highlights how diverse estrangements can be, both in their causes and consequences.

In the introductory chapters, Melvin describes the conscious acts of distancing from family members and what sets these acts apart from other types of separations or relational processes. Perhaps this sets the scene for a book that is predominantly focused on exploring the more conscious aspects of the challenges complex family relationships pose, and the resulting relational void associated with family estrangement.

Melvin cites studies suggesting approximately 1 in 4 estranged people seek clinical help and highlights how, despite this, there appears to be only a small number of training programmes for professionals who work with adults or families who are experiencing estrangement. By reviewing and summarising the research, Melvin makes a valuable contribution towards addressing the lack of awareness of this topic and the potential long-term psychological consequences for individuals who have experienced damaging behaviours within a family, including mental health issues, emotional distress and trauma. Moreover, by combining research findings, Melvin's book offers a collaborative framework for practitioners to understand and manage the complexity of estrangement dynamics when supporting clients to heal from the wounds of broken attachments.

There can be no doubt that after 30 years of painstaking work, the appearance of the Revised Standard Edition of the Complete Psychological Works of Sigmund Freud (RSE), edited by Mark Solms, is a scholarly event of seismic proportions. Within the psychoanalytic community, the RSE surely ranks as the most significant contribution to English language Freud scholarship so far in the twenty-first century. The importance of this new edition is, however, not limited to psychoanalysis, as its impact will reverberate across all areas of research and debate that Freud's work has already so significantly informed and influenced for well over a century. While generations of English language readers have mainly come to know Freud through James Strachey's consummate, if controversial translation, those engaging with Freud's thought will now also do so through Solms' revised translation and the enhanced and updated editorial apparatus that scaffolds it.

Given the significance of what the publication of the RSE means, it is therefore important that some of the implications of the editorial decisions shaping it are indicated, a task I will devote most of this review to. Before doing so, however, readers of the British Journal of Psychotherapy will want some sense of what, exactly, has changed from Strachey's original translation. The first and perhaps principal point to note is given in the title: this is a revised rather than a new translation. As Solms writes in the ‘Preface to the Revised Edition’: ‘The reasoning behind [the] decision’, to revise Strachey's translation rather than to translate Freud anew, ‘revolved mainly around questions of convention, but also the special problems of psychoanalytic terminology, and the limitations of translation itself’ (Solms, RSE 1, p. 59). When translating Freud, Solms reminds us that Strachey opted for the strategy of treating him as if he were an ‘Englishman of science’. The rationale for this is the mutually exclusive choice facing the translator, to ‘either use the conventions of the language being translated from or that being translated into. Neither solution’, Solms says fairly, ‘is better and it is impossible to employ them both: one simply has to make a choice’ (Solms, RSE 1, p. 60). It is worth noting that Jean Laplanche, in preparing the French counterpart to the RSE, the Oeuvres complètes, made the opposite choice, of following German language conventions. As we shall see, these divergent translatory decisions are not neutral, but rather they contribute to far-reaching philosophical and ideological ramifications, such that Solms' election to retain Strachey's treatment of Freud as if he were an ‘Englishman of science’, is of the greatest significance for the ongoing English language reception of Freud.
